title: The $275 Million Turmeric Myth: Why South Asian Kitchens Got It Right and the Supplement Industry Got It Wrong
excerpt: Thirty papers retracted, curcumin barely detectable in the bloodstream, and turmeric supplements are now the top cause of herbal liver injury in the US. Here is what the diaspora needs to know.
body:
For generations, South Asian households have treated turmeric as both spice and medicine. A pinch in dal, a paste on wounds, haldi doodh before bed. The logic was experiential, not clinical: it worked because grandmothers said it worked.

Then Western science arrived at the same conclusion — or seemed to. Starting in the early 2000s, the biochemist Bharat Aggarwal at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center published over 100 papers claiming that curcumin, turmeric's yellow pigment, could reduce inflammation and kill "almost all types" of tumour cells. A New Scientist investigation published this week reveals just how dramatically that research has unravelled — and what it means for the millions of people now spending money on curcumin supplements.

## The Retraction Cascade

In 2012, academic whistleblowers flagged potentially fraudulent results in at least 65 of Aggarwal's papers. MD Anderson launched an internal investigation. Aggarwal left the cancer centre. To date, 30 of his papers have been retracted from scientific journals. Yet his remaining papers continue to be widely cited, and the supplement industry he helped create keeps growing. US health agencies have spent more than $275 million on curcumin research since 1990, much of it following Aggarwal's early work.

The problem extends beyond one researcher. A landmark 2017 review in the *Journal of Medicinal Chemistry*, led by Kathryn Nelson at the University of Minnesota, concluded bluntly that "curcumin is an unstable, reactive, nonbioavailable compound and, therefore, a highly improbable lead" for therapeutic use.

## The Bioavailability Wall

The core issue is chemistry. Curcumin barely dissolves in water, which means the human body struggles to absorb it. A study by Dutch researchers found that curcumin was "barely detectable" in the bloodstreams of men who took supplements — even high doses of enhanced formulations designed to boost absorption with piperine from black pepper or nanoparticle delivery systems. The concentrations found in their blood were more than 100 times lower than those that showed activity against cancer cells in a laboratory dish.

Nelson and her colleagues described curcumin as "a missile that continually blows up on the launch pad, never reaching the atmosphere or its intended targets."

This probably explains why curcumin has failed to show convincing benefits in any rigorous clinical trials for cancer, arthritis, or other conditions that the supplement industry routinely markets it for.

## The Liver Problem Nobody Talks About

More troubling than ineffectiveness is potential harm. According to the US National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, turmeric supplements have become "the most common cause of clinically apparent, herbal-related liver injury in the United States." Most cases are attributed to highly bioavailable forms of curcumin — the enhanced formulations that supplement companies sell at premium prices specifically because they claim to solve the absorption problem.

Symptoms include yellowing of the skin, dark urine, and nausea. While most cases resolve after stopping the supplement, a small number of people have died of liver failure. In Norway and Sweden, a turmeric supplement linked to liver problems and deaths was found to be adulterated with nimesulide, a pain medication.

Separately, more than a dozen brands of ground turmeric in the US were recalled between 2011 and 2016 after they were found to contain lead chromate, added to enhance the spice's colour. Some children who regularly ate food spiced with these products had dangerously high blood lead levels.

## What Your Kitchen Already Knew

Here is the irony that the diaspora will recognise immediately. Turmeric in food is safe. The spice makes up only about five per cent curcumin by dry weight, and when it is cooked into a curry or stirred into warm milk with other spices, the dose is small and mixed with fats and other compounds that the body processes naturally.

The danger emerges when the supplement industry extracts, concentrates, and enhances curcumin into doses that the body was never designed to handle — and sells them at margins that would make a pharma company blush.

The South Asian kitchen, in other words, had the dosage right all along. A pinch in the dal. A half-teaspoon in the doodh. Enough to colour and flavour, not enough to overwhelm. The mistake was not turmeric itself. The mistake was assuming that if a little is good, a capsule full of concentrated extract must be better.

For NRIs who grew up watching their parents cook with turmeric and now see it repackaged as a $40 bottle of capsules at Whole Foods, the message from the latest science is straightforward: keep the haldi in your spice box, skip it in the supplement aisle.

*Sources: New Scientist, Journal of Medicinal Chemistry, US NIDDK, Retraction Watch*
